stage.need: Figuring out a puzzle or a plan at 5 to 7. CDC suggests puzzles, building blocks, simple board and card games with rules and asking 'Why?' and 'How?' at age 5; Nemours KidsHealth says that by 7 it is common for many kids to problem solve in a more organized and logical way; a 2026 review of board-game studies found promising but not yet firm effects on executive functions. Games give a puzzle to work out, books show someone who tries again or finds another way.
stage.age_caveat: Ages are approximate: the KidsHealth line is for 7 year olds, the CDC tips are for 5 year olds, and children differ. The frame says בסביבות and the caption says יש ילדים ש.... The board-game research is promising, not conclusive, so the wording stays at practise and opportunity.

dev_sources.title: Milestones by 5 Years
dev_sources.publisher: CDC, Learn the Signs. Act Early.
dev_sources.quote: Developmental milestones are things most children (75% or more) can do by a certain age. / Play with toys that encourage your child to put things together, such as puzzles and building blocks. / Teach your child to follow rules in games. For example, play simple board games, card games, or Simon Says. / Help her expand her answers by asking "Why?" and "How?"
dev_sources.supports: CDC suggests, for age 5, playing with puzzles and building blocks, simple board and card games with rules, and asking 'Why?' and 'How?'. Read today through WebFetch (CDC blocks plain curl); sentences joined with ' / ', and the tool returned them as extracted text, not a raw HTML copy. Limits: these are parent tips for age 5, not a milestone about problem solving, and the page does not mention thinking ahead or trying another way. The 6-years milestone page returned 404, so CDC covers only up to 5 here. Use for 'around 5, puzzles and games with rules are everyday ways to practise', never for a promised outcome.

dev_sources.title: 7 Year Well-Child Checkup
dev_sources.publisher: Nemours KidsHealth (medically reviewed by Elana Pearl Ben-Joseph, MD, August 2024)
dev_sources.quote: By 7 years, it's common for many kids to: ... have longer attention spans / problem solve in a more organized and logical way
dev_sources.supports: Nemours KidsHealth lists, among common development at 7, longer attention spans and solving problems in a more organized and logical way. Read today by curl; the list items are joined with ' ... ' and ' / ' (the page shows them as bullets). Limits: a general checkup page for parents, 'common for many kids' not a test; it says nothing about games, puzzles, planning ahead or persistence. It supports the general direction at about age 7, not the 5 to 6 end of the range.

dev_sources.title: Can executive functions be improved by playing board games across the lifespan? A systematic review and meta-analysis
dev_sources.publisher: Estrada-Plana et al., Applied Psychology: Health and Well-Being 2026;18(4):e70194, doi:10.1111/aphw.70194 (PubMed, NIH)
dev_sources.quote: In the systematic review, we especially found effects in verbal short-term memory in children. In addition, the meta-analysis showed significant results for visuospatial short-term memory in kindergarten and processing speed in older people. / Overall, the results suggest that the current empirical evidence is not yet sufficient to support a strong recommendation for the use of board games to improve executive functions. However, the findings are promising and highlight the potential of board games as a cognitive intervention.
dev_sources.supports: Peer reviewed review of 24 studies (16 in the meta-analysis): promising but NOT sufficient for a strong recommendation that board games improve executive functions. Effects were in short-term memory (verbal in children; visuospatial in kindergarten), not planning or problem solving as such, and kindergarten is not ages 5 to 7 exactly. Only the abstract was read (PubMed page shows a cookie notice, so the abstract came from NCBI's efetch service for PMID 42532119). Use only as a soft 'research suggests board games are a promising way to exercise thinking skills', never 'prove' or 'improve'.

dev_sources.title: Just Play Cognitive Modern Board and Card Games, It's Going to Be Good for Your Executive Functions: A Randomized Controlled Trial with Children at Risk of Social Exclusion
dev_sources.publisher: Moya-Higueras et al., Children (Basel) 2023;10(9):1492, doi:10.3390/children10091492 (PubMed, NIH)
dev_sources.quote: Sixty-eight participants (7-12 years old) were divided into two experimental groups ... We found significant time effects in cognitive flexibility and inhibition and, to a lesser extent, in working memory in both gaming groups.
dev_sources.supports: Randomized trial, 68 children aged 7 to 12 at risk of social exclusion: cognitive flexibility and inhibition improved over time in both groups that played modern board and card games. Limits: ages 7 to 12 (only the top of our range), a vulnerable population, no non-playing control group in the abstract, and it measured flexibility, inhibition and memory, not planning or problem solving. Only the abstract was read (NCBI efetch for PMID 37761453); sentences joined with ' ... '. Use for 'a chance to practise flexible thinking', never a promised result.

caption:
משחקים וספרים שבהם הילדים מתרגלים לפתור בעיות
קודם המשחקים ואחר כך הספרים
יש ילדים שפותרים בעיות מוקדם ויש שצריכים עוד זמן
מה הילדים שלכם עושים כשנתקעים?

claims.wording_he: משחקים וספרים שיעזרו להם לתרגל פתרון בעיות
claims.supports: CDC suggests puzzles, building blocks and simple board and card games with rules at 5 and asking 'Why?' and 'How?'; KidsHealth: by 7 it is common to solve problems in a more organized and logical way; a 2026 review of 24 studies calls board games promising but not yet strong enough for a firm recommendation. 'Help them practise' is our wording, no result is promised. No source covers picture books.

claims.wording_he: בסביבות גיל 7 הרבה ילדים פותרים בעיות בצורה מסודרת
claims.supports: Nemours KidsHealth, 7 year checkup: by 7 years it is common for many kids to problem solve in a more organized and logical way.

claims.wording_he: חידות ומשחקי חוקים מאפשרים להם לתרגל את זה
claims.supports: CDC for age 5: puzzles and building blocks, simple board and card games. The review of board-game studies found promising but not conclusive effects. 'An opportunity to practise' is our wording, not a promise.

claims.wording_he: מתרגלים לתכנן איזו מאורה לבנות ולנצל את מה שיש להם
claims.supports: HaKubia describes the game as building lairs from resources, developing map reading, using opportunities and negotiation; CDC suggests simple board games with rules at 5. Our reading, not a tested effect of this game.

claims.wording_he: מתרגלים לחשוב איך מגינים על הקלפים שלהם
claims.supports: FoxMind files the game under strategy skills: players wake queens while guarding against dragons and potions. CDC suggests simple card games with rules. Our reading, not a tested effect of this game.

claims.wording_he: מתרגלים לתכנן מסלול ולגלות איפה המסלול נעצר
claims.supports: Kodkod's description: children build different tracks and watch the chain reaction; CDC suggests toys that encourage putting things together. Our reading, not a tested effect of this set.

claims.wording_he: מתרגלים לנסות שוב כשהבנייה לא מצליחה
claims.supports: Sifriyat Pijama's blurb: the girl whose build fails does not give up and tries again and again. No study on picture books was found; CDC suggests asking 'Why?' and 'How?' questions, which the 'how' line uses.

claims.wording_he: מתרגלים לחשוב איך מזיזים אבן ענקית וכבדה
claims.supports: Sifriyat Pijama's blurb: how to move a giant heavy stone from the market square into the king's palace, a story about a big problem and a creative princess. No study on picture books was found; the question line follows CDC's 'How?' tip.

claims.wording_he: מתרגלים להבין איך פותרים חידה בדרך מקורית
claims.supports: Sifriyat Pijama's blurb: how to know which of two is right; a clever girl offers an original way. No study on picture books was found; the question line follows CDC's 'Why?' and 'How?' tip.

claims.wording_he: סיפור מותאם אישית עם תמונה של הילדים שלכם
claims.supports: Live site, 2026-10-16: upload a photo of the child and add the name; the name is in the text and the child stars in every illustration.

claims.wording_he: שבו הם מתאמנים בכדורגל שוב ושוב וממשיכים לנסות
claims.supports: Catalogue book 23 (lumebook.com, 2026-10-16, ages 4 to 8): a story about a child who loves football and discovers persistence; the site says that even after a fall you get up and keep trying. The cover shows a boy of about 7 kicking a ball next to a trophy.

claims.wording_he: מתרגלים למצוא פתרון כששני צדדים תקועים
claims.supports: Sifriyat Pijama's blurb: a bear and a giant meet in the middle of a narrow bridge; their solution shows the advantage of joint thinking and creativity. No study on picture books was found; the question line follows CDC's 'How?' tip.
A closing question to the parents, not a fact. It rests on the frame: by 7 many children problem solve in a more organized way.

notes: Stage solve-it-5-7. Open flags: all seven product images and the LumeBook cover are rights_unverified or owned as noted; the three games were checked on Toys R Us (best-selling sort, 469 products) and the books via Sifriyat Pijama and Steimatzky on 2026-10-16. No study on picture books that model problem solving was found, so the book lines rest on the Sifriyat Pijama blurbs and stay at 'practise'. The LumeBook cover has small brand-like lettering on the pitch boards in the background. Domino Rally is a chain-reaction set, not a board game.
